checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)

tiers.label: Practice player = the strongest program (our best)

names: Standing on its own joints (no walking policy)
Seeing the ball and the wind
Timing at x1: acting on fresh information

skills.name: Stays on its feet
skills.real: No walking policy is given: the program drives every joint; on the platform gains alone a G1 falls within about 1.3 s. A real G1 does not stand without a balance controller, and every serve and receive starts from standing.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: the match record / (2 robots × match minutes), examined only with ≥ 5 own hits (fall_rate). Scenarios base / recv: the same reading.
skills.line: ≤ 2 falls per robot-minute in 2/3 of matches

skills.name: Takes a knock and stays up
skills.real: Collisions with a partner and being pulled off balance after a dive are common in beach volleyball; stable means taking a knock and still standing for the next ball.
skills.measure: Scenario push: the opponent serves every point; 0.3 s after the serve hit one robot of the program's (alternating) gets a sideways push of 1.2 m/s to its pelvis. The scenario record: pushes where the robot stood at the push and did not fall within 2 s (fell = false) / all pushes.

skills.name: Serves legally in still air
skills.real: Every point starts with a serve. A flat palm holds the ball, no fingers, and the server must stand on its own before and after.
skills.measure: Scenario serve: the program serves every point, the wind set to 0. Share of the scenario record (server_side = A) with service_fault = false. Checkpoint Evaluation: the world's serve drill, legal / units.

skills.name: Serves legally in the wind
skills.real: An outdoor sport where floating serves drift. The wind is read only from two windsocks beyond the far side, and the serve must be corrected for it.
skills.measure: Scenario wind: the program serves every point, the wind fixed at 3.0 m/s (direction by seed; inside the official 0-5 m/s). The same reading as serve_calm; examined only when the same program reads ≥ 60 % in the serve scenario. Checkpoint Evaluation: serves in the match (the seed's wind).

skills.name: Watches the serve
skills.real: One fixed head camera tilted 30 deg up, no neck: the robot looks by turning its waist or body. A serve flies 1.2-1.8 s; unseen, it is not received.
skills.measure: Scenario recv (and Checkpoint Evaluations): for each legal serve of the opponent, whether a frame the program received during the flight (serve hit to the next touch / landing; episode observe rows, view_steps) was taken while the ball was inside an own head camera's field of view. Share = serves seen / legal serves.

skills.name: Reaches the serve
skills.real: Receiving is the first test of beach volleyball: see the serve, judge where it comes down, get there and put the arms in place, the whole chain within about 1.5 s.
skills.measure: Scenario recv: the opponent (L2) serves every point. The scenario record: share of legal serves with touch_own_k set (an own robot touched the ball in the point, the referee's touch event). Checkpoint Evaluation: the same reading (opp_touched / flights).

skills.name: Side-out
skills.real: The receiving side wins the point back (side-out); about 60-70 % in elite play.
skills.measure: Scenario recv: share of the points on the opponent's legal serves won by the program (the scenario record, winner = A; the opponent's service faults left out). Checkpoint Evaluation: sideout_rx / opp_legal.

skills.name: Commands keep coming
skills.real: Real time at x1 with 100 Hz control; at the joint layer no walking policy covers a gap, so a robot starts to fall when the commands stop.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation (x1): episode cmd rows, each robot's 95th percentile command gap in play (steps), the mean of the two (cmd_gap_p95). The base scenario (x1, Quest) gives the reference and ablation readings.

open_questions: Move the wind_serve scenario to 5 m/s (at 3 m/s serving without reading the wind is all legal)?

notes.challenge: Two humanoids a side and a ball in the wind. The program finds the ball with one head camera, reads the wind from two windsocks and times every serve and receive in real time.

achieved.text: The serve decided the game: in 34 matches the receiving team won none of about 375 points in which the serve landed in.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash served 0 of 8 legally because its controller swapped the serve for a standing pose once the ball left its hands. Its notes named the bug, and the fixed program served 8 of 8 in the next match.
DeepSeek predicted where serve-only play ends: "first server wins 16-14". Its semifinal against Claude Opus 5.5 went 14:16, with the server winning all 30 points.
Opus's robots fell 170 times in 12 matches yet served 131 of 137; robots are re-placed every point, so falls rarely cost points.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: Its serve passed 200 of 200 seeds in practice before failing live; after the repair it still never won a point on a legal incoming serve (0 of 47).
Kimi 3.1 Pro: Fielded learned return and receive motions in two Open Arena matches, one of the few learned contact skills in the whole event.

interface.sees: One head camera per robot, the G1's real colour camera (424 × 240, a new frame every 10 ms), each robot's joints, balance sensor and position, the wind on the windsocks, and the referee's calls. No ball coordinates.
interface.controls: Targets for all 29 joints of both robots, one row or a plan of up to 300 rows of 10 ms, with optional speeds, torques, stiffness and damping. Real time, 100 times a second.
interface.moment: Final, Claude Opus 5.5 v GPT-6 Astra, match point with Opus ahead 15–14, 1:10 in the replay. Opus's serve is coming over the net; both of Astra's robots see it in their head cameras. Astra's robot 2 (ringed) plays it out, and Opus wins 16–14.

camera.label: Robot cameras · Astra's two robots · 424 × 240 each

details: Cameras: one in each robot's trunk, the real G1's Intel RealSense D435i colour camera, 424 × 240, 69.4° × 42.5°, tilted 30° up. The G1 has no neck, so a robot looks elsewhere by turning its waist, leaning or turning its body.

A new frame every 10 ms; the newest a program can fetch is 20 ms old, both robots' tiles in one image, stamped with their step. To keep the cameras fast, their images leave out the stands and the crowd and draw the sky in flat colours.
Not given: where the ball is. The program finds it in the images; the windsocks show the wind.
Own robots: position, heading, trunk height and lean, velocity, all 29 joint angles and speeds, the pelvis IMU, the targets in force, and whether each robot is down.
Referee: score, set half, clock, situation (service, rally, between rallies), who serves, the 5 s service clock, the hits used on its side, and how the last point was won.

Command, per robot: targets for all 29 joints (or the 17 of waist and arms), one row or up to 300 rows, one per 10 ms step, or a plan for chosen joint groups from a chosen step; optional velocities, feed-forward torques and gains. Targets beyond the joint ranges or speeds are clipped; the joint controller runs every 2 ms through the motors' torque–speed curves.

No ready-made skills: no walking policy, hit or serve. On the default gains alone a robot falls within about 1.3 s. The ball rests on the server's left palm; the program tosses and strikes it within 5 s of the whistle.
Timing: a control step every 10 ms; the match runs at real speed and never waits; commands for both robots sent together act on the same step.
Rules: FIVB beach volleyball, 2 v 2 on an 8.4 × 4.2 m court, three hits a side, one set to 15 (at 16-all the next point wins), with wind.
Before the match: 2 hours of preparation with a full practice copy of the court, a practice opponent and a GPU training kit (half an RTX PRO 6000).
